Newly fertilised eggs of the Common sea star (Asterias rubens) proceed through early cleavage and blastula formation while still suspended in the water column following broadcast fertilisation. Embryonic development proceeds rapidly under warmer conditions; at 16 °C [T = 16 °C], the age at birth, defined as the moment when the free-swimming bipinnaria larva hatches from the fertilised ovum, is approximately 4 days [ab = approximately 4 days]. The total length at birth of these newly hatched larvae is remarkably small, measuring just 0.027 cm [Lb = 0.027 cm], a size that reflects the minimal yolk reserves provisioned within each egg. This diminutive starting dimension necessitates a prolonged period of planktotrophic feeding before the larva attains the size threshold required for the next major developmental transition. The bipinnaria larva feeds actively on phytoplankton, undergoing a series of growth stages that culminate in the formation of a competent brachiolaria larva capable of substratum attachment. These early life-history parameters are consistent with observations from other north Atlantic asteriid species, where small larval size at hatching is linked to high fecundity and a reliance on exogenous food resources from the onset of the exotrophic phase.

Following a period of active growth in the plankton, the bipinnaria larva of Asterias rubens reaches a critical developmental milestone when it acquires metamorphic competence. The time since birth at metamorphosis, measured from the moment of hatching to the onset of larval settlement and body plan reorganisation, has been documented as 81 days  when larvae are reared at a constant temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. This relatively extended larval phase reflects the energetic demands of building the adult rudiment and accumulating sufficient reserves for the drastic morphological transformation to come. At the point of metamorphic climax, the larva settles onto a suitable substratum and undergoes arm resorption, with the diameter at metamorphosis, measured across the newly emerged post-larval juvenile, being approximately 0.4 cm . This measurement includes the tube feet that are already functional at settlement; without the podia, the disc diameter is closer to 2 mm. The juvenile that emerges from this transformation is a miniature, five-armed starfish that immediately begins benthic foraging. This size at settlement is broadly comparable to values reported for other members of the family Asteriidae.

The post-metamorphic juvenile phase is characterised by rapid somatic growth and the gradual differentiation of the reproductive system. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the time since birth at puberty, marked by the first visible onset of gonad maturation, has been recorded at 120 days [tp = 120 days]. At this point, individuals have typically attained a diameter at puberty of approximately 2 cm [Lp = approximately 2 cm], measured from arm tip to arm tip across the central disc. This size threshold represents a key life-history transition, as it signals the shift from exclusive investment in somatic growth to the initiation of gametogenesis. The attainment of puberty at this relatively small body size is ecologically meaningful, as it allows individuals to begin contributing to the next generation within their first year of life, provided environmental conditions are favourable. The onset of reproductive activity is likely influenced by food availability and local population density, with individuals in resource-rich habitats potentially maturing at a slightly smaller size. In contrast, the species is known to achieve considerably larger dimensions as fully grown adults.

Reproductively active adults of Asterias rubens are capable of sustained gamete production over multiple spawning seasons. At a stable temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of the species has been estimated by combining observations of fecundity per spawning event and spawning frequency. Individual females release between approximately 2.5 million and 2.5 million eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 2.5 million and 2.5 million eggs per spawning event], a prodigious output that is typical of broadcast-spawning echinoderms. Field and laboratory records indicate that a single female may spawn once annually [F_R_i = single female may spawn once annually], though the exact frequency can vary with local thermal regimes and food supply. This high fecundity is an essential life-history strategy for a species with a small, vulnerable larva that faces substantial mortality during its extended planktonic phase. Under optimal conditions, the combination of a very large clutch size with an annual spawning cycle yields a substantial annual reproductive output. The benefits of this strategy are evident in the species' broad distribution and ecological success across the North Atlantic and adjacent Arctic waters.

As individuals of Asterias rubens advance in age, growth rates decelerate and individuals approach their ultimate size. The ultimate total length, measured from the tip of the longest arm to the tip of the opposite arm, has been reported as 52 cm [Li = 52 cm] in some exceptionally large specimens, although Brig1983 gives a more typical maximum of 40 cm for North Sea populations. This considerable arm span makes Asterias rubens one of the larger predatory sea stars in its region. At a constant temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the maximum recorded life span for the species is 1095 days [am = 1095 days], though longevity in the wild is likely influenced by predation pressure, disease, and the energetic costs of reproduction. This lifespan of approximately three years is relatively modest for an echinoderm, particularly when compared to some deep-sea asteroids that may live for several decades. The comparatively short life span is coupled with a high reproductive output, a classic r-selected life-history strategy that favours rapid maturation and high fecundity over extended somatic persistence. The species' demographic profile is thus shaped by a trade-off between early reproduction and a relatively brief adult phase.
